planting.note: Plant dormant canes in late winter to early spring; as a primocane-fruiting cultivar it can bear a fall crop on first-year canes the same season it is planted, in addition to a floricane crop the following spring. Unlike its later thornless University of Arkansas descendants, Prime-Jim retains thorns.

directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained, fertile soil and provide a simple wire support for the upright, thorny canes. Released in 2004 alongside Prime-Jan by the University of Arkansas breeding program, Prime-Jim was the first primocane-fruiting (fall-bearing) blackberry cultivar ever developed, a genetic breakthrough that made possible the later thornless Prime-Ark series. It produces two crops from one planting: a conventional floricane harvest in early summer and a second primocane harvest on new canes in late summer and fall. Remove all canes to the ground after the fall harvest if only the primocane crop is wanted, or leave canes standing over winter to also collect the following spring's floricane crop.
sources: University of Arkansas Division of Agriculture — Primocane Blackberry Breeding Program
North Carolina State University Extension — Primocane-Fruiting Blackberries
University of Georgia Extension — Fall-Bearing Blackberry Varieties

planting.note: Plant rooted tip-layered cuttings or crowns in late winter to early spring on a low two-wire trellis; Lucretia ripens several weeks ahead of upright blackberries, extending the bramble harvest into late spring before summer heat sets in.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, sandy loam and train the sprawling, thorny canes onto a low trellis or wire to keep the large fruit off the ground. Lucretia is one of the oldest named dewberry cultivars still grown in the South, prized in Texas and the Gulf region in the early twentieth century for producing unusually large, glossy, sweet-tart fruit far earlier in the season than blackberries. Because dewberries flower and ripen so early, protect blossoms from late cold snaps and expect a short, intense harvest window rather than the extended cropping of modern blackberry cultivars. Cut spent floricanes to the ground after harvest to keep the sprawling planting from becoming an unmanageable thicket.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Dewberries and Blackberries for the Home Garden
LSU AgCenter — Bramble Fruits for Louisiana
USDA historical small fruit variety records

common_name: Ebony King Dewberry (Heirloom Self-Fruitful Southern Dewberry)

planting.note: Plant rooted tip cuttings or crowns in late winter to early spring on a low trellis; Ebony King was historically favored over other heirloom dewberries because a single planting sets a full crop without a separate pollinator variety nearby.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained, moderately fertile soil and train the trailing, thorny canes onto a low wire trellis to keep fruit clean and easy to pick. Ebony King is an early twentieth-century Southern dewberry selection once popular from Texas through the Gulf South for its dependable, self-fruitful cropping and glossy black, firm, sweet-tart berries that ripen ahead of blackberry season. It largely fell out of commercial favor as upright, easier-to-manage blackberry cultivars became available, but it remains a hardy, low-input option for gardeners wanting the distinctive early-season flavor of a true dewberry. Cut fruited canes to the ground after harvest and train new primocanes onto the trellis for the following year's crop.
sources: Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Dewberries and Blackberries for the Home Garden
LSU AgCenter — Bramble Fruits for Louisiana
USDA historical small fruit variety records

common_name: Merton Thornless Blackberry (Historic English Thornless Blackberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant canes or container stock in early spring on a sturdy trellis; the semi-trailing, thornless canes need tying in through the season since they do not stand upright on their own.

directions: Plant in full sun in deep, well-drained soil and train the vigorous, semi-trailing canes onto a two-wire trellis, tying in new growth through the growing season. Bred in England from a thornless mutation, Merton Thornless was one of the first commercially grown thornless blackberry cultivars and became the parent of many later thornless releases, including some of the early Arkansas breeding lines. Fruit is medium-sized, glossy black, and moderately firm with a classic tart-sweet blackberry flavor, ripening in mid-to-late summer. Prune out spent floricanes to the ground after harvest and select the strongest new canes to retie for the following season.
sources: Oregon State University Extension — Growing Blackberries in the Home Garden
Royal Horticultural Society — Blackberry Cultivars
Washington State University Extension — Small Fruit Production Guide

common_name: Oregon Thornless Blackberry (Thornless Cutleaf Evergreen Blackberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant canes on a sturdy trellis in early spring; the long trailing canes are vigorous and need firm tying and regular pruning to keep the planting contained.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil and provide a strong trellis for the long, trailing, thornless canes, which are more vigorous than most upright blackberry cultivars. Oregon Thornless is a thornless sport of the cutleaf or 'Evergreen' blackberry, distinguished by deeply cut, fern-like leaflets that give the plant an almost ornamental appearance in addition to its fruit crop. Berries are medium-sized, firm, and tart, ripening late in the season and holding well on the vine after ripening. Because canes are highly vigorous and can root wherever tips touch soil, prune hard after harvest and keep tips off the ground to prevent the planting from spreading beyond its trellis.
sources: Oregon State University Extension — Growing Blackberries in the Home Garden
Washington State University Extension — Small Fruit Production Guide

common_name: Latham Raspberry (Classic Cold-Hardy Heirloom Red Raspberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root canes in early spring as soon as soil can be worked; Latham needs a substantial winter chill and performs best in cold-winter regions rather than the Gulf South.

directions: Plant bare-root canes in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil and support rows with a simple two-wire trellis. Released by the University of Minnesota in the 1920s, Latham became one of the most widely planted red raspberries in the northern United States for decades because of its exceptional winter hardiness and reliable, heavy midsummer crop of firm, bright red berries with classic tart-sweet raspberry flavor. It is a floricane-fruiting type, bearing on second-year canes, so remove spent canes to the ground right after harvest and thin new primocanes to the sturdiest 4-6 per foot of row. Modern cultivars have surpassed it in disease resistance, but Latham remains valued in cold climates for its toughness and long track record.
sources: University of Minnesota Extension — Raspberries for Home Gardens
North Dakota State University Extension — Growing Raspberries
Michigan State University Extension — Raspberry Cultivars

common_name: Boyne Raspberry (Extreme Cold-Hardy Manitoba Red Raspberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root canes in early spring; Boyne requires a long, cold winter chill and is best suited to northern gardens rather than warm, low-chill regions.

directions: Plant bare-root canes in full sun in well-drained, fertile soil and provide a simple wire trellis for support. Developed at the Morden Research Station in Manitoba, Boyne is prized in the coldest raspberry-growing regions of North America for surviving harsh prairie winters with minimal cane dieback while still producing an early, heavy crop of medium-sized, firm, richly flavored red berries. As a floricane-fruiting cultivar it bears on second-year wood, so cut spent canes to the ground immediately after harvest and thin the following year's primocanes to keep the row open and productive. Its combination of hardiness and early ripening has made it a long-standing standard for home gardeners across the northern Great Plains and Canadian Prairies.
sources: University of Minnesota Extension — Raspberries for Home Gardens
North Dakota State University Extension — Growing Raspberries
Government of Manitoba Agriculture — Small Fruit Production

common_name: Tulameen Raspberry (Premium Late-Season British Columbia Raspberry)

planting.note: Plant dormant bare-root canes in early spring on a sturdy trellis; Tulameen has a long midsummer ripening window and canes benefit from support given the weight of the large fruit.

directions: Plant bare-root canes in full sun in deep, fertile, well-drained soil and support the tall canes on a two-wire trellis. Bred in British Columbia, Tulameen is a premium fresh-market red raspberry known for unusually large, firm, glossy berries with excellent sweet flavor and a notably long harvest window that extends well into late summer. It is a floricane-fruiting type, so remove spent canes to the ground after the season and thin new primocanes to the strongest shoots to maintain fruit size and quality. Because the canes are tall and heavily laden when fruiting, secure them well to the trellis to prevent wind and fruit-weight breakage.
sources: British Columbia Ministry of Agriculture — Raspberry Production Guide
Washington State University Extension — Small Fruit Production Guide
Oregon State University Extension — Raspberry Cultivars
